      "kind": "issue",
      "status": "open",
      "body": "NOTE APPENDED 2026-07-26 (run 0048 round 2): item 3's "cheaper option" is REFUTED; the
human question in this item STANDS and is still yours.

REFUTED: "relaxing just the chart-wise partitions to a joint covering drops the requirement
from two avoided points to ONE.  Worth trying before anyone builds PGL_2."  It buys nothing,
and the reason is a typing fact, not a failed proof.  FinCoverData types its pieces INTO the

`pieces := Sum.elim (basicOpen . h0) (basicOpen . h1)` (:186) -- so every piece is a basic
open of one of the two PINNED charts by construction, whatever the partition data says.
Per-piece swallow-or-miss already holds for any cover by opens (DivSchemeCertZarConn.lean:98
uses only openness), so a connected divisor still lands in one piece, and `basicOpen_le` puts
that piece inside one chart.  Changing the partition FIELDS cannot change where the pieces
LIVE.  Recorded as roadmap leaf ...ddr.certificate.joint-cover, status rejected, with the
10-file rebuild cost if anyone tries it anyway.

The sharp form to quote from now on: NO repair that keeps the pieces inside the preimages of
a FIXED PAIR of points of P^1 can work.  Only R1 (vary the pinned pair -- needs Aut(P^1)) or
R2 (generalize the piece type) remain.

STILL OPEN AND STILL YOURS: over a small finite field, where |P^1(k)| = q + 1 < n + 2, what
is DivFamZar supposed to be?  Nothing in the three options below has changed.

--- ORIGINAL ---
CORRECTION TO MY ANSWER ON I-0333, filed in the same round after an adversarial pass. The
NEGATIVE half of that answer stands unchanged: chart-avoid is NO, decisively, and you do not
have to take that decision. The POSITIVE half — "the repair is cheap and it is not a decision" —
was too optimistic in three ways, and one of them puts a DIFFERENT question back to you.

WHAT SURVIVED. The Z(diamond) chart does not confine its divisors; the counterexample is real;
the obstruction is DivEq-invariant and therefore bites DivFamZar itself; confinement is an open
condition on the base, so an atlas may legitimately record avoidance. All kernel-checked or
argued in informal/spec-dd-r.md ADDENDUM 3.

WHAT DID NOT.
 1. The counterexample is FIELD-INDEPENDENT (irreducibility of s(x^2+1)+x needs nothing of k),
    so it also kills the "assume k infinite" escape I proposed. Enlarging the field does not
    help.
 2. The repair RELOCATES the forbidden geometric input rather than removing it: fibrewise-finite
    support is not implied by anything a LocalEquations carries, and must be discharged from the
    seed's own degree data.
 3. My diagnosis "the binding constraint is FinCoverData" was too narrow. Per-piece
    swallow-or-miss follows from (c1)-finiteness for ANY cover by opens; only the chart-wise

    requirement from two avoided points to ONE. Worth trying before anyone builds PGL_2.

THE QUESTION THAT IS NOW YOURS, and it is a different one from I-0333's:

  OVER A SMALL FINITE FIELD, WHERE |P^1(k)| = q + 1 < n + 2, WHAT IS DivFamZar SUPPOSED TO BE?

Certifiability needs two k-rational points of P^1 off the support's image at every base point.
Challenge.lean:96-99 states the Jacobian over an ARBITRARY field, and nothing in Picard/ or
RiemannRoch/ assumes more than [Field k]. Three options, not comparable on mathematical grounds
alone:
 (a) accept |P^1(k)| >= n + 2 as a hypothesis and record that the challenge as stated is then
     not solved for small q;
 (b) plan a descent lane — divQProj (Picard/DivSchemeQProj.lean) is the right lever for fpqc
     descent from a big enough k'/k;
 (c) generalize the pinned charts to closed points of degree d >= 2, paying
     Gamma(P1 k, chartOpen k i) iso Polynomial k (Curve/P1Charts.lean:234,239) and
     isPrincipalIdealRing_chartSections (Curve/P1Points.lean:64), since Cl(P^1 minus a degree-d
     point) = Z/d.

Roadmap leaf: AJCR.w4-rep.datum.dat-d.ddr.certificate.field-size (blocked, high). It should be
settled BEFORE anyone builds the GL_2(k) action on P^1 (leaf p1-aut) — it decides whether that

      "id": "I-0348",
      "kind": "issue",
      "status": "open",
      "body": "**CORRECTED 2026-07-26 (run 0048 round 2): the headline claim is WRONG. The file PARSES.**

",

Established 2026-07-26 (run 0048 round 2) by two independent adversarial audits, and it is
the single highest-value generalizable lesson from four rounds of recon on AJCR.

The pattern: a module docstring lists "Main declarations" that the file never declares; a

    file has no olean, ilean, trace or hash, so nothing in it has ever been checked.

RULE: before briefing a lane, or writing a roadmap row, or quoting a "cheap item", run
  /home/axel/.archon-env/bin/horizon search "<name>" --json
and require a hit with a signature.  One second per claim.  Apply this to your own
docstrings too: do not announce a theorem you have not declared.",

   the base locus of K, so the hypothesised exact-pole generator exists iff the conclusion
   already holds. Circular.

   irreducible degree-2 relative Cartier divisor whose fibre at s = 0 is {0, infinity}, and it
   stays irreducible over every nonempty open of the base. s(x^2+1) + x is degree 1 in s with
   coprime coefficients over ANY field, so this works over F_2. Consequence: "assume k infinite"
   is NOT an escape from the obstruction, and small finite fields are a genuine hole in every
   avoidance-based repair. (The example was already in the tree as a docstring model at
   Picard/DivSchemeCertZarConn.lean:170-175.)

3. THE OBSTRUCTION NEEDS NO CONNECTIVITY. isClosed_supportLocus_inter_chart_of_isCertified
   (Picard/DivSchemeCertZarConfine.lean, landed this round): a certificate forces BOTH pinned
   chart traces closed, full stop. Use this form, not the preconnected one, when refuting.
   And it is DivEq-invariant (DivEq.supportLocus_eq, same file), so it bites the DivFamZar
   QUOTIENT — re-spelling the equations is not an escape either.

4. TWO CONSTRAINTS, NOT ONE. (c1)-finiteness = leak-freeness gives per-piece swallow-or-miss for
   ANY cover by opens, so a connected support lies inside a single PIECE no matter how
   FinCoverData is reshaped. Only the chart-wise partitions of unity (DivisorFamily.lean:174,176)
   upgrade that to a single CHART. Sharp form: no repair keeping pieces inside the preimages of
   a FIXED PAIR of points of P^1 can work. UNTRIED CHEAP OPTION: relax the partitions to a joint
   ⨆ pieces = top — drops the requirement from two avoided points to one.

5. DEAD END, with a reason: deleting clause (c1) from IsCertified. Module.Flat R (colength j) is
   free from fibrewise regularity alone (flat_colength_of_forall_tmul_residueField,
   SupportTube.lean:313 — no finiteness, no no-leak), so it looks like finiteness is the only
   culprit. It is not usable: every (c2)/(c3)/(c4) keystone in SlicingFlatKernel.lean (variable
   block :221-224) carries [Module.Finite R M] with M = chartProd, which IS finite colengths.

   [IsFinite pi], [IsDominant pi], [IsAffineHom pi] and the propositional triangle hpi; DivScheme
   (DivScheme.lean:144) takes two abstract CurveDivisors and pi enters only at the instantiation.
   So a coordinate twist needs no atlas gluing. But Aut(P^1) does not exist in this project, and
   mathlib has Proj.map without Proj.mapIso; and the project has no k-rational points of P^1 at
   all.",

---
name: blueprint-conventions
description: The LaTeX-subset blueprint format and house style — environments, \uses/\lean/\leanok/\mathlibok/\notready, the math-purity rule, and complete (not sketched) proofs.
---

Blueprints are a LaTeX subset (the `leanblueprint` dialect) parsed into the DAG.
Write timeless mathematics — a standalone document, not a project journal.

## Environments

Each declaration is an amsthm-style environment; the recognized ones are
`theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, `definition`, `remark`,
`example`, `notation`, `convention`, and `proof`. A statement environment plus
its following `proof` environment form one node's content.

## Per-node macros

- `\label{id}` — a stable id (the DAG node key).
- `\lean{Name}` — the Lean declaration(s) this node formalizes; comma-separate to
  bind several (`\lean{a, b}`) when they jointly formalize the node's statement.
  Each named declaration's signature must match the statement. The mapping need
  not be 1-to-1: a node may name several declarations, and Lean may carry
  auxiliary declarations with no node at all.
- `\uses{a,b}` — dependencies on other nodes' labels; these drive the DAG edges.
  Add an edge instead of re-explaining a dependency in prose. Put `\uses` in the
  statement for definitional deps and in the `proof` for deps used only in the
  proof.
- `\source{slug:page-0001}` — reference anchors for UI popups and audit trails.
  Use page-level ids from `references/<slug>/tex/page-0001.tex` or an equivalent
  manifest entry. Multiple anchors may be comma-separated.
- `\leanok` — the Lean is written and checked. Honest only when its Lean is
  actually checked *and* its dependencies are too. On a `proof`, it means the
  proof is formalized; on a statement, the signature is formalized.
- `\mathlibok` — the declaration is already available in mathlib (no
  formalization needed; treat as a leaf).

## House style

- **Pure mathematics only.** No Lean tactics, typeclass/implementation notes, or
  semi-Lean pseudocode. No project history ("since iter N", "our failed route")
  and no conversational filler. Not every Lean helper needs its own node —
  auxiliary or implementation-only declarations can stay unnoded; add a node when
  the result is mathematically meaningful in its own right. In particular, never
  add a `Formalization note` paragraph to blueprint `.tex`: attach implementation
  details, failed approaches, and mechanization caveats to the statement's hgraph
  node with `horizon graph ... add comment` instead.
- **Complete proofs, not sketches.** A node's `proof` is a real, rigorous
  mathematical proof a reader could check — not a hand-wave or a TODO. The way to
  keep it short is to *split*, not to abbreviate: if a proof is long or a node
  grows past a short paragraph, break out the hard step as its own `\uses`-linked
  lemma (down to sentence-sized lemmas if needed) so each node stays small and
  its proof stays complete.
- **One statement's worth per node.** Keep each node to a single mathematical
  statement; don't restate Lean source as prose.
- **Cite by source link, not quote comments.** Add `\source{...}` to the
  relevant node. Keep the retrieved/transcribed page text in `references/` (for
  example `references/<slug>/tex/page-0042.tex`) and let the UI expose it; do not
  paste verbatim source quotes into `% QUOTE` comments inside the blueprint.

---
name: hgraph
description: The dependency graph — Horizon's vendored hgraph core keeps one file per statement/Lean declaration under <project>/hgraph/; `horizon graph frontier` ranks work and agents attach node-scoped comments and reviews. This is the only DAG engine.
---

Each project may carry an **hgraph**: a plain-files semantic graph under
`<project>/hgraph/` — one Markdown node per blueprint statement and per Lean
declaration, typed edges (`uses` = the hard dependency DAG, `formalizes` =
informal↔formal identity). `horizon graph sync` (run automatically at run boundaries)
reconciles the blueprint + Lean sources into it; your **authored** additions
(comments, reviews, metadata) are never touched by sync. The files are
committed to the workspace ledger like everything else.

Use `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …`; when a workspace has one project,
`-p` is optional. Address nodes by `label:<latex-label>` or
`decl:<lean-fqname>` — raw ids are opaque hashes. Most commands accept `--json`.

## Sync it yourself — and act on the warnings

Don't wait for the run boundary: after you change blueprint statements,
`\uses{}`/`\lean{}` annotations, or Lean declarations, run
`"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> sync` and **read its output**. Sync prints warnings for exactly the defects
you can fix on the spot: `\uses{X} has no blueprint node` (missing/mistyped
label), `\lean{Name} not found in Lean sources` (renamed or unwritten
declaration), stale nodes whose source vanished. Fix what your change caused
before moving on; a warning you deliberately leave (e.g. a forward reference
you'll write next) gets a node comment or a memory item so the next session
knows it's intentional. Sync is idempotent and never touches your authored
comments/reviews/metadata.

## Read

- `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> list --state ready` — nodes whose dependencies are all closed:
  provable *now*. Other states: `closed`, `blocked`, `formalized_open`.
- `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` — the ready nodes ranked by how many downstream nodes a
  proof would unlock. **Use this when picking the next node to prove.**
- `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:thm:foo` — one node: statement, `lean_status`
  (`lean_ok | mathlib_ok | sorry | empty`, derived from scanning the Lean, not
  from `\leanok`), deps, attached comments/reviews.
- `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> ancestors label:thm:foo` — the dependency cone.
- `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> stats` — per-state counts for the project.

## Write — per-node progress lives WITH the node

- **Comment = failure memory / progress note on that node.** When an approach
  fails or you learn something node-specific, record it where the next session
  will look first:
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> add comment label:thm:foo --content "tried simp+ring, fails because …"`
  Agent authorship plus run/session/task provenance are filled from the run
  environment; do not copy the note into the blueprint.
- **Review = a Maths / Lean verdict** (independent axes, `good|bad`):
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> add review label:thm:foo --maths good --lean bad --lean-comment "statement ok; proof has a sorry at the succ case"`
- **Metadata**: `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> modify node label:thm:foo --set status=verified`

Prefer node comments over inbox items for anything scoped to ONE node; use the
inbox (skill: `horizon-inbox`) for cross-node or cross-session coordination.

An edge `source --uses--> target` means *source depends on target*. A node is
"ready" when all of its dependencies are closed; prefer `frontier`, which ranks
ready nodes by what they unlock. The dashboard provides the workspace project
switcher and the chapter-collapsed Graphviz view.

## Relation to the blueprint

The DAG **is** the hgraph — there is no second engine and no parser fallback.
It is generated by resolving the blueprint's `\uses{}`/`\lean{}` annotations
against the real Lean sources, so keeping those annotations correct (skill:
`blueprint-conventions`) is exactly what keeps this graph correct. Unresolved
references surface as `horizon graph sync` warnings and as `dangling` entries — read
the warnings rather than trusting `dangling` alone.

---
name: references
description: The shared workspace-root references/ library and its manifest.yaml — how to find, read, and cite original sources with \source{...}. Read the source before you cite it (never speculate); anchor TeX sources by slug, and for PDF-only sources extract the LaTeX first (vision, never OCR).
---

`references/` is a **shared library at the workspace root** — one library for
every project — holding the original source material a blueprint is formalised
from (papers, books, notes). It is indexed by `references/manifest.yaml`. Per-
project files live under each project's directory; `references/` does not — it is
always at the workspace root, and `references/**` is writable from any agent.

A blueprint node derived from a source carries a `\source{...}` anchor. Those
anchors are the audit trail from a formal statement back to where it came from,
so they must be **true**, not plausible.

## The one rule: read before you cite

**Never add a `\source{...}` anchor to a source you have not actually read.** Do
not infer a citation from a title, a topic, a theorem number, or your own prior
knowledge of the result. An anchor asserts "this exact statement/proof appears
here" — if you haven't opened the referenced material and confirmed it, you don't
know that, and a wrong anchor is worse than none (it sends the next reader/agent
to the wrong place and launders a guess as provenance).

Concretely, before writing `\source{...}`:
1. Confirm the source exists in `references/manifest.yaml`. If it isn't there,
   get it in first (see below) — don't cite a slug that doesn't resolve.
2. Open the actual content — the TeX, or the transcribed page — and confirm the
   statement/proof you're anchoring is really there.
3. Only then write the anchor.

## Anchor forms — pick by what the source actually is

The manifest's `read` field for each entry tells you which case you're in.

- **The source has LaTeX** (arXiv e-print, an open `.tex`, etc.): read the TeX
  directly and cite the source as a whole — `\source{slug}`. Do **not** invent a
  `page-NNNN`; a TeX source has no rendered pages, so a page number would be
  fabricated. If the manifest documents stable sub-ids for the source (a section
  or label id), you may use `\source{slug:<id>}`, but only an id that exists.
- **The source is PDF-only** (no usable TeX): cite the transcribed page,
  `\source{slug:page-NNNN}`, where `page-NNNN` is a real file under
  `references/<slug>/tex/page-NNNN.tex` that you have read. If that page hasn't
  been transcribed yet, transcribe it first (below) — don't cite a page that
  doesn't exist on disk.

Multiple anchors may be comma-separated: `\source{slug:page-0042, other:page-0007}`.

## Getting a source into the library

Don't fetch and stash sources ad hoc. Spawn the **`reference-retriever`** subagent
(by name, through your engine's native subagent mechanism) with whatever you have
— topic, arXiv ID, DOI, title, URL, target page range. It downloads the original
(preferring TeX, keeping the PDF), verifies the file is real (not a paywall/login
page named `.pdf`), organises it under `references/<slug>/`, and registers it in
`references/manifest.yaml`. Wait for it, then cite from what it wrote.

## Extracting the LaTeX from a PDF-only source

When there is no reliable TeX and you need the actual math (to read it, or to cite
a page), **extract it with the proper tool — don't eyeball the PDF and paraphrase.**
The extraction path is the **`page-transcriber`** subagent, which renders each page
to an image and **vision-transcribes** it into one self-contained
`references/<slug>/tex/page-NNNN.tex` per page.

- **Vision, never OCR.** OCR mangles math (subscripts, operators, alignment);
  reading the rendered page image with a vision model preserves it. This is a hard
  rule of the transcription flow.
- **A small vision model is usually enough.** Faithful page transcription doesn't
  need a frontier model — a cheap vision-capable model typically suffices. The
  Horizon agent chooses the model and effort at dispatch time; do not encode that
  spend policy in `config.yaml` or the descriptor.
- **Keep each call ≤5 pages.** Longer ranges lose accuracy; split a big range
  across several `page-transcriber` calls.

## Reading transcriptions correctly

- A transcribed page is `references/<slug>/tex/page-NNNN.tex` where `NNNN` is the
  **PDF page index**, which often differs from the printed page number. The
  manifest entry's `read` field records the `page_offset` and any fallback that
  actually worked — respect it when mapping "Theorem 3.4 on p. 12" to a file.
- Read the whole page file before citing it; a page can hold several results.

## The manifest at a glance

One entry per source (the `reference-retriever` owns the full schema):

```yaml
references:
  - slug: <slug>
    title: <title>
    source: <arXiv ID / DOI / URL>
    status: ok            # or: not_found
    files:
      - { path: <slug>/<slug>.pdf, format: pdf }
      - { path: <slug>/source.tex, format: tex }        # if TeX obtained
      - { path: <slug>/tex/page-0042.tex, format: tex } # if transcribed
    read: "Read TeX when present; else page anchors slug:page-NNNN. page_offset: ..."
```

   871	\section{Wiring for the positive-genus Albanese witness}
   872	\label{sec:albaneseup_witness_wiring}
   873	
   874	\cref{thm:albanese_universal_property} supplies the universal-factorisation
   875	field \(\texttt{isAlbaneseFor}\) of an Albanese witness for \((C, P_0)\) in the
   876	sense of \cref{def:JacobianWitness} (\cref{chap:Jacobian}); the remaining
   877	fields are supplied by A.3:

   879	  \item \(J := \Pic^0_{C/k}\) (the underlying scheme).
   880	  \item \(\texttt{grpObj}\): the group-object structure on \(J\) obtained from the
   881	    abelian-group structure on \(\Pic^0_{C/k}(T)\) for varying \(T\), refined to a
   882	    group object in the category of \(\bar k\)-schemes (A.3, A.2.c group-scheme

   333	the Abel--Jacobi morphism \(\iota_{P_0}\) at the basepoint \(P_0\). It is the

   378	  C \times \{P_0\}\bigr)\) is the rigidified diagonal correspondence on
   379	  \(C \times C\) and \(\mathcal M^{P_0}\) is the Poincar\'e--Picard correspondence
   380	  on \(C \times J\).
   381	\end{lemma}
   382	
   383	% SOURCE QUOTE PROOF: (no separate verbatim source; the existence of
   384	% \(f^P\) is part of Milne's standing setup at the head of \S III.6 -- ``\(J\)
   385	% will be its Jacobian variety'' -- and is the moduli-of-degree-0-line-bundles
   386	% interpretation of \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) packaged into Summary~6.11.)
   387	\begin{proof}
   388	  
   389	  By A.3, \(J := \Pic^0_{C/k}\) is the moduli scheme of degree-zero line bundles
   390	  on \(C\); concretely, for every \(\bar k\)-scheme \(T\) its \(T\)-points are
   391	  isomorphism classes of line bundles \(\mathcal L\) on \(C \times_{\bar k} T\)
   392	  whose fibre degree at every geometric point of \(T\) is zero, taken modulo line
   393	  bundles pulled back from \(T\) (the universal property of the Picard scheme
   394	  packaged in \cref{def:pic_scheme}; the identity component imposes the
   395	  degree-zero condition).
   396	
   397	  Apply this to \(T := C\) and the line bundle
   398	  \[
   399	    \mathcal L^{P_0} \;:=\; \mathcal O_{C \times_{\bar k} C}\bigl(\Delta -
   400	      \{P_0\} \times C - C \times \{P_0\}\bigr),
   401	  \]
   402	  the rigidified diagonal correspondence on \(C \times_{\bar k} C\). Its fibre
   403	  over a \(\bar k\)-point \(Q \in C(\bar k)\) along the second projection is the
   404	  degree-zero line bundle \(\mathcal O_C(Q - P_0)\) on \(C\), so \(\mathcal L^{P_0}\)
   405	  is a relative degree-zero line bundle, hence a \(C\)-point of \(J\). The
   406	  representability of \(J\) at \(T = C\) produces the unique morphism
   407	  \[
   408	    \iota_{P_0} \;\colon\; C \;\longrightarrow\; J
   409	  \]
   410	  such that \((1 \times \iota_{P_0})^*\mathcal M^{P_0} \approx \mathcal L^{P_0}\)
   411	  for the Poincar\'e--Picard correspondence \(\mathcal M^{P_0}\) on \(C \times J\).
   412	
   413	  At the basepoint, restriction of \(\mathcal L^{P_0}\) to \(C \times \{P_0\}\)
   414	  gives \(\mathcal O_C(P_0 - P_0) \cong \mathcal O_C\), the trivial line bundle,
   415	  whose moduli class in \(J(\bar k)\) is the identity element \(\eta_J\). Hence
   416	  \(\iota_{P_0}(P_0) = \eta_J\). Uniqueness of \(\iota_{P_0}\) is the moduli
   417	  uniqueness clause of representability: any other morphism \(\iota'_{P_0}\)
   418	  satisfying \((1 \times \iota'_{P_0})^*\mathcal M^{P_0} \approx \mathcal L^{P_0}\)
   419	  and the pointed condition agrees with \(\iota_{P_0}\) on \(T\)-points for every
   420	  \(T\), hence equals \(\iota_{P_0}\) by the Yoneda embedding.
   421	\end{proof}

   424	\label{sec:albaneseup_sym_g}

   426	The Albanese universal property is built from \(C\) by taking the
   427	\(g\)-th \emph{symmetric power} \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) -- the quotient of the
   428	\(g\)-fold Cartesian power \(C^g\) by the natural action of the symmetric group
   429	\(S_g\). We collect the definition here as the first sub-lemma block.

   462	  \(\bar k\) and let \(g \ge 1\). The \emph{\(g\)-th symmetric power}

   493	\section{The induced morphism on the symmetric power}
   494	\label{sec:albaneseup_sym_g_av_map}
   495	
   496	The second sub-lemma is the elementary fact that the symmetric assignment
   497	\((P_1, \ldots, P_g) \mapsto \varphi(P_1) + \cdots + \varphi(P_g)\) from
   498	\(C^g\) to \(A\) descends through \(\pi \colon C^g \to \mathrm{Sym}^g C\). The
   499	key point is that the addition morphism \(A^g \to A\) is itself
   500	\(S_g\)-symmetric because \(A\) is commutative as a group scheme.
   501	
   502	\begin{lemma}\leanok
   503	[Symmetrisation of a curve-to-AV morphism]
   504	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_av_map}
   505	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.symmetricPowerAVMap}
   506	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve}
   507	
   508	  % SOURCE: [Milne, Abelian Varieties], Proof of Proposition~6.1, \S III.6,
   509	  % doc p.~104 (read from references/abelian-varieties.pdf, PDF page 110).
   510	  % SOURCE QUOTE:
   511	  % "PROOF.  Consider the map
   512	  %     \((P_1,...,P_g)\mapsto\sum_i\psi(P_i)\colon C^g\to A.\)
   513	  %  Clearly this is symmetric, and so it factors through \(C^{(g)}\)."
   514	  \textit{Source: Milne, \emph{Abelian Varieties}, Proof of Proposition~6.1,
   515	  \S III.6, p.~104.}
   516	
   517	  Let \(\varphi \colon C \to A\) be a morphism into an abelian variety \(A\)
   518	  over \(\bar k\). The composition
   519	  \[
   520	    \mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g}
   521	    \;\colon\; C^g \;\longrightarrow\; A^g \;\longrightarrow\; A,
   522	    \qquad (P_1, \ldots, P_g) \;\longmapsto\; \varphi(P_1) + \cdots + \varphi(P_g),
   523	  \]
   524	  is \(S_g\)-equivariant (where \(S_g\) acts on \(C^g\) by permutation of the
   525	  factors and on \(A\) trivially). Consequently, by the universal property of
   526	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) (\cref{def:symmetric_power_curve}), there is a unique
   527	  morphism of \(\bar k\)-schemes
   528	  \[
   529	    \mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \;\colon\; \mathrm{Sym}^g C \;\longrightarrow\; A
   530	  \]
   531	  such that
   532	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \circ \pi = \mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g}\).
   533	\end{lemma}
   534	
   535	\begin{proof}
   536	  
   537	  Since \(A\) is a commutative group scheme, the \(g\)-fold addition morphism
   538	  \(\mathrm{add}_A \colon A^g \to A\) satisfies \(\mathrm{add}_A \circ \tau =
   539	  \mathrm{add}_A\) for every \(\tau \in S_g\) permuting the factors of \(A^g\)
   540	  (this is the scheme-theoretic statement that summation in a commutative
   541	  monoid is independent of the order of summands; on \(T\)-points it is the
   542	  identity \(a_1 + \cdots + a_g = a_{\tau(1)} + \cdots + a_{\tau(g)}\) in the
   543	  abelian group \(A(T)\)). The diagonal action of \(\tau\) on \(\varphi^{\times
   544	  g} \colon C^g \to A^g\) is also given by permutation of factors. Therefore
   545	  \[
   546	    (\mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g}) \circ \tau
   547	    \;=\; \mathrm{add}_A \circ (\varphi^{\times g} \circ \tau)
   548	    \;=\; \mathrm{add}_A \circ (\tau \circ \varphi^{\times g})
   549	    \;=\; (\mathrm{add}_A \circ \tau) \circ \varphi^{\times g}
   550	    \;=\; \mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g},
   551	  \]
   552	  so the composition \(\mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g}\) is symmetric
   553	  in the sense of \cref{def:symmetric_power_curve}. The universal property
   554	  of \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) produces the unique factorisation
   555	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \colon \mathrm{Sym}^g C \to A\).
   556	\end{proof}

   684	\begin{lemma}\leanok

    59	\section{Setup and statement}
    60	\label{sec:albaneseup_setup}
    61	
    62	Fix an algebraically closed field \(\bar k\) and a smooth proper geometrically
    63	irreducible curve \(C\) over \(\bar k\) of genus \(g = g(C) > 0\) (the positive-genus
    64	hypothesis is essential: it is precisely the standing hypothesis of Milne's
    65	\S III.6). Fix moreover a \(\bar k\)-rational point \(P_0 \in C(\bar k)\) to serve
    66	as the basepoint of the Albanese construction.
    67	
    68	By the A.3 row of Route~A (the identity-component construction applied to the
    69	representable Picard scheme of
    70	\cref{def:pic_scheme} in \cref{chap:Picard_FGAPicRepresentability}) the
    71	identity component \(\Pic^0_{C/k} \subseteq \Pic_{C/k}\) is a smooth proper
    72	geometrically irreducible \(\bar k\)-group scheme of dimension \(g\); we write
    73	\(J := \Pic^0_{C/k}\) and let \(\eta_J \colon \Spec \bar k \to J\) denote its
    74	identity section, in the project's convention the chosen \(\mathbf 1\)-pointed
    75	morphism that represents the unit element of the underlying group object on
    76	\(J\).
    77	
    78	The universal \(T\)-points of \(J\) are degree-\(0\) line bundles on \(C \times_{\bar k}
    79	T\), taken modulo line bundles pulled back from \(T\) (\cref{chap:Picard_LineBundlePullback};
    80	the identity component then refines this to the degree-zero subfunctor on the
    81	\'etale sheafification). This moduli interpretation is what underlies the
    82	Abel--Jacobi morphism \(\iota_{P_0} \colon C \to J\) of
    83	\cref{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism}. The universal homomorphism \(\psi \colon J
    84	\to A\) corresponding to a pointed morphism \(\varphi \colon C \to A\) is
    85	constructed by Milne's symmetric-power route: the symmetric assignment
    86	\((P_1, \ldots, P_g) \mapsto \varphi(P_1) + \cdots + \varphi(P_g)\) defines a
    87	regular morphism \(\widetilde \psi \colon \mathrm{Sym}^g C \to A\), the
    88	birational morphism \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C \dashrightarrow J\) inverts to a
    89	rational map \(J \dashrightarrow A\), and the rational-map extension theorem
    90	\cref{thm:rational_map_to_av_extends} promotes that rational map to the
    91	desired regular morphism \(\psi\).
    92	
    93	The goal of the chapter is to establish:
    94	
    95	\begin{theorem}
    96	[Albanese universal property of \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) -- Milne III~\S 6, Proposition~6.1]
    97	  \label{thm:albanese_universal_property}
    98	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.albanese_universal_property}
    99	  \uses{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism, lem:symmetric_product_av_map, lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian, lem:descent_through_birational_sigma, lem:albanese_eq_iff_symmetricPower_eq, thm:rational_map_to_av_extends, thm:rigidity_lemma}
   100	
   101	  % SOURCE: [Milne, Abelian Varieties], Proposition~6.1, \S III.6, doc p.~104
   102	  % (read from references/abelian-varieties.pdf, PDF page 110).
   103	  % SOURCE QUOTE:
   104	  % "PROPOSITION 6.1. Let \(P\) be a \(k\)-rational point on \(C\).  The map
   105	  %  \(f^P\colon C\,\to\,J\) has the following universal property: for any
   106	  %  map \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) from \(C\) into an abelian variety sending
   107	  %  \(P\) to \(0\), there is a unique homomorphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\) such
   108	  %  that \(\varphi=\psi\circ f^P\)."
   109	  \textit{Source: Milne, \emph{Abelian Varieties}, Proposition~6.1, \S III.6, p.~104.}
   110	
   111	  Let \(C\) be a complete nonsingular curve of genus \(g > 0\) over an algebraically
   112	  closed field \(\bar k\), let \(P_0 \in C(\bar k)\) be a \(\bar k\)-rational point,
   113	  and write \(J := \Pic^0_{C/k}\), \(\iota_{P_0} \colon C \to J\) for the
   114	  Abel--Jacobi morphism of \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism}. Then for every
   115	  abelian variety \(A\) over \(\bar k\) and every pointed morphism
   116	  \(\varphi \colon C \to A\) with \(\varphi(P_0) = \eta_A\), there exists a unique
   117	  homomorphism of group schemes \(\psi \colon J \to A\) such that
   118	  \(\varphi = \psi \circ \iota_{P_0}\).
   119	\end{theorem}

   146	\begin{lemma}\leanok

   148	  \label{lem:isReduced_of_flat_of_surjective}

   150	
   151	  Let \(\pi \colon Y \to X\) be a flat, surjective morphism of schemes (i.e.\

   153	\end{lemma}

   156	  Fix \(x \in X\) and choose \(y \in Y\) with \(\pi(y) = x\). The induced
   157	  local ring homomorphism on stalks \(\mathcal O_{X,x} \to \mathcal O_{Y,y}\)
   158	  is flat and local, hence faithfully flat, hence injective. Since
   159	  \(\mathcal O_{Y,y}\) is reduced (as \(Y\) is reduced) and a subring of a
   160	  reduced ring is reduced, \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\) is reduced. As \(x\) was
   161	  arbitrary, \(X\) is reduced.
   162	\end{proof}

    21	`φ(P₀) = η_A` factors uniquely as `φ = ψ ∘ ι_{P₀}` for a homomorphism of
    22	group schemes `ψ : Pic⁰_{C/k̄} ⟶ A`.

   116	Following the project (cf. `AbelianVarietyRigidity.lean`, `Jacobian.lean`),
   117	an **abelian variety over `k̄`** is encoded as an object
   118	`A : Over (Spec (.of k̄))` carrying the four instances:
   119	
   120	- `[GrpObj A]` (group-object structure on the over-category),
   121	- `[IsProper A.hom]` (complete),
   122	- `[Smooth A.hom]` (nonsingular),
   123	- `[GeometricallyIrreducible A.hom]` (geometrically irreducible).
   124	
   125	A **smooth proper geometrically irreducible curve over `k̄`** carries:
   126	
   127	- `[SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 C.hom]`,
   128	- `[IsProper C.hom]`,
   129	- `[GeometricallyIrreducible C.hom]`.
   130	
   131	These instances are supplied by `inferInstance` at the call site.

   330	\label{sec:albaneseup_abel_jacobi}

   337	\begin{lemma}\leanok
   338	[Abel--Jacobi morphism at a basepoint]
   339	  \label{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism}
   340	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.abelJacobi}
   341	  \uses{def:pic_scheme, def:jacobian_scheme}
   342	
   343	  % SOURCE: [Milne, Abelian Varieties], \S III.6, the canonical map
   344	  % \(f^P\colon C\to J\) (introduction to Proposition~6.1), doc p.~104
   345	  % (read from references/abelian-varieties.pdf, PDF page 110).
   346	  % SOURCE QUOTE:
   347	  % "PROPOSITION 6.1. Let \(P\) be a \(k\)-rational point on \(C\).  The map
   348	  %  \(f^P\colon C\to J\) has the following universal property: for any map
   349	  %  \(\varphi\colon C\to A\) from \(C\) into an abelian variety sending \(P\)
   350	  %  to \(0\), there is a unique homomorphism \(\psi\colon J\to A\) such that

   352	  % SOURCE: [Milne, Abelian Varieties], \S III.6, Summary 6.11, doc p.~107
   353	  % (read from references/abelian-varieties.pdf, PDF page 113).
   354	  % SOURCE QUOTE:
   355	  % "SUMMARY 6.11.  Between \((C,P)\) and itself, there is a divisorial
   356	  %  correspondence \(\mathcal L^P = \mathcal L(\Delta-\{P\}\times C-C\times\{P\})\).
   357	  %    Between \((C,P)\) and \(J\) there is the divisorial correspondence
   358	  %  \(\mathcal M^P\); for any divisorial correspondence \(\mathcal L\) between
   359	  %  \((C,P)\) and a pointed \(k\)-scheme \((T,t)\), there is a unique morphism
   360	  %  of pointed \(k\)-schemes \(\varphi\colon T\to J\) such that
   361	  %  \((1\times \varphi)^*\mathcal M^P\approx \mathcal L\).  In particular,
   362	  %  there is a unique map \(f^P\colon C\to J\) such that
   363	  %  \((1\times f^P)^*\mathcal M^P\approx \mathcal L^P\) and \(f(P)=0\)."

   367	  Let \(C\) be a complete nonsingular curve of genus \(g > 0\) over \(\bar k\), let
   368	  \(P_0 \in C(\bar k)\) be a basepoint, and write \(J := \Pic^0_{C/k}\). There is a
   369	  unique regular morphism of \(\bar k\)-schemes
   370	  \[
   371	    \iota_{P_0} \;\colon\; C \;\longrightarrow\; J, \qquad
   372	    Q \;\longmapsto\; \bigl[\mathcal O_C(Q - P_0)\bigr],
   373	  \]
   374	  sending the basepoint \(P_0\) to the identity element \(\eta_J \in J(\bar k)\)
   375	  and characterised on \(T\)-points by the formula
   376	  \((1 \times \iota_{P_0})^*\mathcal M^{P_0} \approx \mathcal L^{P_0}\), where
   377	  \(\mathcal L^{P_0} := \mathcal O_{C \times C}\bigl(\Delta - \{P_0\} \times C -
   378	  C \times \{P_0\}\bigr)\) is the rigidified diagonal correspondence on
   379	  \(C \times C\) and \(\mathcal M^{P_0}\) is the Poincar\'e--Picard correspondence

   382	
   383	% SOURCE QUOTE PROOF: (no separate verbatim source; the existence of
   384	% \(f^P\) is part of Milne's standing setup at the head of \S III.6 -- ``\(J\)
   385	% will be its Jacobian variety'' -- and is the moduli-of-degree-0-line-bundles
   386	% interpretation of \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) packaged into Summary~6.11.)
   387	\begin{proof}
   388	  
   389	  By A.3, \(J := \Pic^0_{C/k}\) is the moduli scheme of degree-zero line bundles
   390	  on \(C\); concretely, for every \(\bar k\)-scheme \(T\) its \(T\)-points are
   391	  isomorphism classes of line bundles \(\mathcal L\) on \(C \times_{\bar k} T\)
   392	  whose fibre degree at every geometric point of \(T\) is zero, taken modulo line
   393	  bundles pulled back from \(T\) (the universal property of the Picard scheme
   394	  packaged in \cref{def:pic_scheme}; the identity component imposes the
   395	  degree-zero condition).
   396	
   397	  Apply this to \(T := C\) and the line bundle
   398	  \[
   399	    \mathcal L^{P_0} \;:=\; \mathcal O_{C \times_{\bar k} C}\bigl(\Delta -
   400	      \{P_0\} \times C - C \times \{P_0\}\bigr),
   401	  \]
   402	  the rigidified diagonal correspondence on \(C \times_{\bar k} C\). Its fibre
   403	  over a \(\bar k\)-point \(Q \in C(\bar k)\) along the second projection is the
   404	  degree-zero line bundle \(\mathcal O_C(Q - P_0)\) on \(C\), so \(\mathcal L^{P_0}\)
   405	  is a relative degree-zero line bundle, hence a \(C\)-point of \(J\). The
   406	  representability of \(J\) at \(T = C\) produces the unique morphism
   407	  \[
   408	    \iota_{P_0} \;\colon\; C \;\longrightarrow\; J
   409	  \]
   410	  such that \((1 \times \iota_{P_0})^*\mathcal M^{P_0} \approx \mathcal L^{P_0}\)
   411	  for the Poincar\'e--Picard correspondence \(\mathcal M^{P_0}\) on \(C \times J\).
   412	
   413	  At the basepoint, restriction of \(\mathcal L^{P_0}\) to \(C \times \{P_0\}\)
   414	  gives \(\mathcal O_C(P_0 - P_0) \cong \mathcal O_C\), the trivial line bundle,
   415	  whose moduli class in \(J(\bar k)\) is the identity element \(\eta_J\). Hence
   416	  \(\iota_{P_0}(P_0) = \eta_J\). Uniqueness of \(\iota_{P_0}\) is the moduli
   417	  uniqueness clause of representability: any other morphism \(\iota'_{P_0}\)
   418	  satisfying \((1 \times \iota'_{P_0})^*\mathcal M^{P_0} \approx \mathcal L^{P_0}\)
   419	  and the pointed condition agrees with \(\iota_{P_0}\) on \(T\)-points for every
   420	  \(T\), hence equals \(\iota_{P_0}\) by the Yoneda embedding.
   421	\end{proof}

   423	\section{The \(g\)-th symmetric power \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\)}
   424	\label{sec:albaneseup_sym_g}
   425	
   426	The Albanese universal property is built from \(C\) by taking the
   427	\(g\)-th \emph{symmetric power} \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) -- the quotient of the
   428	\(g\)-fold Cartesian power \(C^g\) by the natural action of the symmetric group
   429	\(S_g\). We collect the definition here as the first sub-lemma block.
   430	
   431	\begin{definition}\leanok
   432	[Symmetric power of a curve]
   433	  \label{def:symmetric_power_curve}
   434	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.SymmetricPower}
   435	  % SOURCE: [Milne, Abelian Varieties], Proposition~3.1, \S III.3,
   436	  % doc p.~94 (read from references/abelian-varieties.pdf, PDF page 100).
   437	  % SOURCE QUOTE:
   438	  % "For any variety \(V\), the symmetric group \(S_r\) on \(r\) letters acts on
   439	  %  the product of \(r\) copies \(V^r\) of \(V\) by permuting the factors, and
   440	  %  we want to define the \(r\)th symmetric power \(V^{(r)}\) of \(V\) to be the
   441	  %  quotient \(S_r \backslash V^r\).  The next proposition demonstrates the
   442	  %  existence of \(V^{(r)}\) and lists its main properties.
   443	  %    A morphism \(\varphi\colon V^r\to T\) is said to be {\bf symmetric} if
   444	  %  \(\varphi\sigma=\varphi\) for all \(\sigma\) in \(S_r\).
   445	  %  PROPOSITION 3.1. Let \(V\) be a variety over \(k\).  Then there exists a
   446	  %  variety \(V^{(r)}\) and a symmetric morphism \(\pi\colon V^r\to V^{(r)}\)
   447	  %  having the following properties:
   448	  %    (a) as a topological space, \((V^{(r)},\pi)\) is the quotient of \(V^r\)
   449	  %        by \(S_r\);
   450	  %    (b) for any open affine subset \(U\) of \(V\), \(U^{(r)}\) is an open
   451	  %        affine subset of \(V^{(r)}\) and
   452	  %             $\Gamma(U^{(r)},\mathcal O_{V^{(r)}}) = \Gamma(U^r,
   453	  %             \mathcal O_{V^r})^{S_r}$
   454	  %        (set of elements fixed by the action of \(S_r\)).
   455	  %  The pair \((V^{(r)},\pi)\) has the following universal property: every
   456	  %  symmetric \(k\)-morphism \(\varphi\colon V^r\to T\) factors uniquely
   457	  %  through \(\pi\).
   458	  %  The map \(\pi\) is finite, surjective, and separable."
   459	  \textit{Source: Milne, \emph{Abelian Varieties}, Proposition~3.1, \S III.3, p.~94.}
   460	
   461	  Let \(C\) be a complete nonsingular curve over an algebraically closed field
   462	  \(\bar k\) and let \(g \ge 1\). The \emph{\(g\)-th symmetric power}
   463	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) is a \(\bar k\)-scheme equipped with a finite surjective
   464	  symmetric morphism \(\pi \colon C^g \to \mathrm{Sym}^g C\) characterised by
   465	  the following universal property: for every \(\bar k\)-scheme \(T\) and every
   466	  symmetric \(\bar k\)-morphism \(\varphi \colon C^g \to T\) (i.e.\ a morphism
   467	  satisfying \(\varphi \circ \sigma = \varphi\) for all \(\sigma \in S_g\)
   468	  acting by permutation of the factors of \(C^g\)) there exists a unique
   469	  morphism \(\overline\varphi \colon \mathrm{Sym}^g C \to T\) with
   470	  \(\overline\varphi \circ \pi = \varphi\). As a topological space
   471	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) is the quotient of \(C^g\) by \(S_g\), and for every open
   472	  affine \(U \subseteq C\) the open subset \(U^{(g)} \subseteq \mathrm{Sym}^g
   473	  C\) is affine with global sections the \(S_g\)-invariants
   474	  \(\Gamma(U^g, \mathcal O_{C^g})^{S_g}\).
   475	\end{definition}

   672	\section{Descent through the birational quotient}
   673	\label{sec:albaneseup_descent}
   674	
   675	The final auxiliary lemma packages the two-step descent that promotes a
   676	morphism on \(C^g\) (after passing through \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) via
   677	\cref{lem:symmetric_product_av_map} and inverting \(f^{(g)}\) via
   678	\cref{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian}) to a regular morphism on
   679	\(J\). The output is a rational map \(J \dashrightarrow A\), which is then
   680	upgraded to a regular morphism via Milne's Theorem~3.2
   681	(\cref{thm:rational_map_to_av_extends}). This is the unique step of the
   682	proof that consumes A.4.c.
   683	
   684	\begin{lemma}\leanok
   685	[Descent of \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi\) to a regular morphism \(J \to A\)]
   686	  \label{lem:descent_through_birational_sigma}
   687	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.descentThroughBirationalSigma}
   688	  \uses{lem:symmetric_product_av_map, lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian,
   689	        thm:rational_map_to_av_extends}
   690	
   691	  % SOURCE: [Milne, Abelian Varieties], Proof of Proposition~6.1, \S III.6,
   692	  % doc p.~104 (read from references/abelian-varieties.pdf, PDF page 110).
   693	  % SOURCE QUOTE:
   694	  % "It therefore defines a rational map \(\psi\colon J\to A\), which (I 3.2)
   695	  %  shows to be a regular map."
   696	  \textit{Source: Milne, \emph{Abelian Varieties}, Proof of Proposition~6.1,
   697	  \S III.6, p.~104 (the sentence ``which (I~3.2) shows to be a regular
   698	  map'').}
   699	
   700	  Let \(\varphi \colon C \to A\) be a morphism into an abelian variety \(A\)
   701	  over \(\bar k\). Let \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \colon \mathrm{Sym}^g C \to A\)
   702	  be the symmetrised morphism of \cref{lem:symmetric_product_av_map} and
   703	  \(f^{(g)} \colon \mathrm{Sym}^g C \to J\) the birational morphism of
   704	  \cref{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian}. Then there is a unique
   705	  regular morphism
   706	  \[
   707	    \psi \;\colon\; J \;\longrightarrow\; A
   708	  \]
   709	  such that \(\psi \circ f^{(g)} = \mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi\) on the dense open
   710	  on which \(f^{(g)}\) is an isomorphism (equivalently, \(\psi\) is the unique
   711	  regular morphism extending the rational map
   712	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \circ (f^{(g)})^{-1} \colon J \dashrightarrow
   713	  A\)).
   714	\end{lemma}
   715	
   716	\begin{proof}
   717	  
   718	  By \cref{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian}, there exist dense opens
   719	  \(U \subseteq \mathrm{Sym}^g C\) and \(V \subseteq J\) with \(f^{(g)}|_U \colon
   720	  U \xrightarrow{\sim} V\) an isomorphism. Setting \(\psi_0 \colon V \to A\)
   721	  to be the composition \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi|_U \circ (f^{(g)}|_U)^{-1}
   722	  \colon V \to U \to A\) produces a rational map \(J \dashrightarrow A\).
   723	
   724	  The target \(A\) is an abelian variety and the source \(J\) is smooth over
   725	  \(\bar k\) (it is itself an abelian variety, hence nonsingular). Milne's
   726	  Theorem~3.2 (\cref{thm:rational_map_to_av_extends}) therefore promotes
   727	  \(\psi_0\) to a unique regular morphism \(\psi \colon J \to A\) extending
   728	  \(\psi_0\) on \(V\). Uniqueness of \(\psi\) follows from the
   729	  reduced-and-separated agreement principle: two regular morphisms
   730	  \(J \to A\) agreeing on a dense open are equal.
   731	\end{proof}

   502	\begin{lemma}\leanok
   503	[Symmetrisation of a curve-to-AV morphism]
   504	  \label{lem:symmetric_product_av_map}
   505	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.Pic0.symmetricPowerAVMap}
   506	  \uses{def:symmetric_power_curve}
   507	
   508	  % SOURCE: [Milne, Abelian Varieties], Proof of Proposition~6.1, \S III.6,
   509	  % doc p.~104 (read from references/abelian-varieties.pdf, PDF page 110).
   510	  % SOURCE QUOTE:
   511	  % "PROOF.  Consider the map
   512	  %     \((P_1,...,P_g)\mapsto\sum_i\psi(P_i)\colon C^g\to A.\)
   513	  %  Clearly this is symmetric, and so it factors through \(C^{(g)}\)."
   514	  \textit{Source: Milne, \emph{Abelian Varieties}, Proof of Proposition~6.1,
   515	  \S III.6, p.~104.}
   516	
   517	  Let \(\varphi \colon C \to A\) be a morphism into an abelian variety \(A\)
   518	  over \(\bar k\). The composition
   519	  \[
   520	    \mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g}
   521	    \;\colon\; C^g \;\longrightarrow\; A^g \;\longrightarrow\; A,
   522	    \qquad (P_1, \ldots, P_g) \;\longmapsto\; \varphi(P_1) + \cdots + \varphi(P_g),
   523	  \]
   524	  is \(S_g\)-equivariant (where \(S_g\) acts on \(C^g\) by permutation of the
   525	  factors and on \(A\) trivially). Consequently, by the universal property of
   526	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) (\cref{def:symmetric_power_curve}), there is a unique
   527	  morphism of \(\bar k\)-schemes
   528	  \[
   529	    \mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \;\colon\; \mathrm{Sym}^g C \;\longrightarrow\; A
   530	  \]
   531	  such that
   532	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \circ \pi = \mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g}\).
   533	\end{lemma}

   535	\begin{proof}
   536	  
   537	  Since \(A\) is a commutative group scheme, the \(g\)-fold addition morphism
   538	  \(\mathrm{add}_A \colon A^g \to A\) satisfies \(\mathrm{add}_A \circ \tau =
   539	  \mathrm{add}_A\) for every \(\tau \in S_g\) permuting the factors of \(A^g\)
   540	  (this is the scheme-theoretic statement that summation in a commutative
   541	  monoid is independent of the order of summands; on \(T\)-points it is the
   542	  identity \(a_1 + \cdots + a_g = a_{\tau(1)} + \cdots + a_{\tau(g)}\) in the
   543	  abelian group \(A(T)\)). The diagonal action of \(\tau\) on \(\varphi^{\times
   544	  g} \colon C^g \to A^g\) is also given by permutation of factors. Therefore
   545	  \[
   546	    (\mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g}) \circ \tau
   547	    \;=\; \mathrm{add}_A \circ (\varphi^{\times g} \circ \tau)
   548	    \;=\; \mathrm{add}_A \circ (\tau \circ \varphi^{\times g})
   549	    \;=\; (\mathrm{add}_A \circ \tau) \circ \varphi^{\times g}
   550	    \;=\; \mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g},
   551	  \]
   552	  so the composition \(\mathrm{add}_A \circ \varphi^{\times g}\) is symmetric
   553	  in the sense of \cref{def:symmetric_power_curve}. The universal property
   554	  of \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) produces the unique factorisation
   555	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \colon \mathrm{Sym}^g C \to A\).
   556	\end{proof}

   586

   588	`φ : C ⟶ A` into an abelian variety `A` with `φ(P₀) = η_A`, there
   589	exists a unique regular morphism `ψ : Pic⁰_{C/k̄} ⟶ A` such that

   597	
   598	/-- **Albanese universal property of `Pic⁰_{C/k̄}` — Milne III §6
   599	Proposition 6.1.**
   600	
   601	For a complete nonsingular curve `C` of genus `g > 0` over an
   602	algebraically closed field `k̄`, a marked `k̄`-point `P₀ ∈ C(k̄)`, and
   603	every pointed morphism `φ : C ⟶ A` into an abelian variety `A` with
   604	`φ(P₀) = η_A`, there exists a *unique* regular morphism
   605	`ψ : Pic⁰_{C/k̄} ⟶ A` such that `φ = ι_{P₀} ≫ ψ`.
   606	
   607	Proof sketch (Milne III.6.1):
   608	1. **Symmetrisation.** `(P₁,…,P_g) ↦ φ(P₁) + ⋯ + φ(P_g)` is
   609	   `S_g`-symmetric (`A` commutative), so factors through
   610	   `Sym^g C` as `Sym^g φ` (`lem:symmetric_product_av_map`).

    12	# The Albanese universal property of `Pic⁰_{C/k}` (A.4.d)
    13	
    14	This file is the **A.4.d** file-skeleton sub-build chapter for the project's
    15	positive-genus arm of `nonempty_jacobianWitness`. It packages Milne's
    16	*Abelian Varieties* §III.6 Proposition 6.1: for a complete nonsingular curve
    17	`C` of genus `g > 0` over an algebraically closed field `k̄` and a marked
    18	`k̄`-point `P₀ ∈ C(k̄)`, the Abel–Jacobi morphism
    19	`ι_{P₀} : C ⟶ Pic⁰_{C/k̄}` is the **Albanese morphism** of the pointed curve
    20	`(C, P₀)`: any pointed morphism `φ : C ⟶ A` into an abelian variety with
    21	`φ(P₀) = η_A` factors uniquely as `φ = ψ ∘ ι_{P₀}` for a homomorphism of
    22	group schemes `ψ : Pic⁰_{C/k̄} ⟶ A`.
    23	
    24	The chapter commits to the **symmetric-power route** (cube-free): the
    25	symmetric assignment `(P₁,…,P_g) ↦ φ(P₁) + ⋯ + φ(P_g)` factors through
    26	`Sym^g C`, the resulting morphism `Sym^g φ : Sym^g C ⟶ A` descends through
    27	the birational morphism `f^{(g)} : Sym^g C ⟶ Pic⁰_{C/k̄}` to a rational map
    28	`Pic⁰_{C/k̄} ⇢ A`, and Milne's Theorem I.3.2 (`extend_to_av` in the sibling
    29	`Albanese/Thm32RationalMapExtension.lean`, A.4.c) promotes it to a regular
    30	morphism `ψ : Pic⁰_{C/k̄} ⟶ A`. The group-homomorphism property of `ψ` then
    31	follows from `ψ(η_J) = η_A` together with Milne Corollary I.1.2 (a
    32	consequence of `thm:rigidity_lemma`).

   114	## Abelian-variety conventions

   116	Following the project (cf. `AbelianVarietyRigidity.lean`, `Jacobian.lean`),

628	\begin{proof}
   629	
   630	  Symmetry of \(\mathrm{add}_J \circ \iota_{P_0}^{\times g}\) is the
   631	  specialisation of \cref{lem:symmetric_product_av_map} to the abelian
   632	  variety \(A := J\) and the morphism \(\varphi := \iota_{P_0}\); the universal
   633	  property of \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) produces the regular morphism \(f^{(g)}\).
   634	  The closed-form description on \(\bar k\)-points,
   635	  \(f^{(g)}(P_1, \ldots, P_g) = [\mathcal O_C(P_1 + \cdots + P_g - g P_0)]\),
   636	  follows because \(\iota_{P_0}(P_i) = [\mathcal O_C(P_i - P_0)]\) by
   637	  \cref{lem:abel_jacobi_morphism} and the group law on \(J\) is the
   638	  tensor-product of degree-zero line bundles.
   639	
   640	  We verify birationality. The image of \(f^{(g)}\) in \(J\) is the iterated
   641	  sum \(\iota_{P_0}(C) + \cdots + \iota_{P_0}(C)\) (\(g\) summands), which is
   642	  closed (it is the image of the proper morphism
   643	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C \to J\), \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\) being proper because \(C^g\)
   644	  is proper and \(\pi\) is finite surjective). By the dimension count
   645	  \(\dim \mathrm{Sym}^g C = g = \dim J\) (Riemann--Roch and the standing
   646	  hypothesis \(g > 0\)), the image \(W^g \subseteq J\) has dimension at most
   647	  \(g\), and equality forces \(W^g = J\) since \(J\) is irreducible. Hence
   648	  \(f^{(g)}\) is surjective with \(\dim\)-equal source and target.
   649	
   650	  For the generic-fibre identification, Riemann--Roch
   651	  \(h^0(D) - h^1(D) = \deg(D) + 1 - g\) at \(\deg D = g\) gives \(h^0(D) - h^1(D)
   652	  = 1\), so for a general \(D \in \mathrm{Sym}^g C(\bar k)\) with \(h^1(D) =
   653	  0\) (the locus where \(h^1\) jumps is closed of positive codimension on a
   654	  smooth curve, by upper semicontinuity of cohomology), we have \(h^0(D) =
   655	  1\) and the linear system \(|D|\) consists of \(D\) alone. Therefore the
   656	  fibre of \(f^{(g)}\) over the generic point of \(J\) contains a single point
   657	  \(D\), i.e.\ \(f^{(g)}\) is birational onto \(J\).
   658	
   659	  By \cref{def:pic_scheme} the underlying \(\bar k\)-scheme \(J\) is the
   660	  Picard scheme \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\) obtained at A.3, so the moduli-theoretic
   661	  reading of \(f^{(g)}\) (effective divisor class \(\mapsto\) degree-zero
   662	  line bundle class via \(D \mapsto [\mathcal O_C(D - g P_0)]\)) is the
   663	  same as the Yoneda image of the \(\mathrm{Sym}^g C\)-point
   664	  \([\mathcal O_{C \times \mathrm{Sym}^g C}(\mathcal D_g - g\{P_0\} \times
   665	  \mathrm{Sym}^g C)]\), where \(\mathcal D_g \subseteq C \times \mathrm{Sym}^g
   666	  C\) is the universal effective Cartier divisor of degree \(g\) on \(C\). We
   667	  do not need this Yoneda repackaging for the proof of the Albanese UP --
   668	  the symmetric-power route uses only the morphism \(f^{(g)}\) and its
   669	  birationality.
   670	\end{proof}

   673	\label{sec:albaneseup_descent}
   674	
   675	The final auxiliary lemma packages the two-step descent that promotes a

   679	\(J\). The output is a rational map \(J \dashrightarrow A\), which is then
   680	upgraded to a regular morphism via Milne's Theorem~3.2

   698	  map'').}

   700	  Let \(\varphi \colon C \to A\) be a morphism into an abelian variety \(A\)
   701	  over \(\bar k\). Let \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \colon \mathrm{Sym}^g C \to A\)
   702	  be the symmetrised morphism of \cref{lem:symmetric_product_av_map} and
   703	  \(f^{(g)} \colon \mathrm{Sym}^g C \to J\) the birational morphism of
   704	  \cref{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian}. Then there is a unique
   705	  regular morphism
   706	  \[
   707	    \psi \;\colon\; J \;\longrightarrow\; A
   708	  \]

   710	  on which \(f^{(g)}\) is an isomorphism (equivalently, \(\psi\) is the unique
   711	  regular morphism extending the rational map
   712	  \(\mathrm{Sym}^g \varphi \circ (f^{(g)})^{-1} \colon J \dashrightarrow
   713	  A\)).
   714	\end{lemma}

   718	  By \cref{lem:symmetric_product_to_jacobian}, there exist dense opens

   720	  U \xrightarrow{\sim} V\) an isomorphism. Setting \(\psi_0 \colon V \to A\)

\paragraph{Corollary 5.5.}
\textit{For all $r \le g$, $f^r \colon C^r \to W^r$ has degree $r!$.}

\paragraph{Proof.}

\paragraph{Remark 5.6.}
(a) The theorem shows that $J$ is the unique abelian variety birationally
equivalent to $C^{(g)}$. This observation is the basis of Weil's construction
of the Jacobian. (See \S 7.)

(b) The exact sequence in (5.1b) can be regarded as a geometric statement of
the Riemann-Roch theorem (see especially the end of the proof). In fact it is
possible to prove the Riemann-Roch theorem this way (see Mattuck and Mayer
1963).

(c) As we observed above, the fibre of
$f^{(r)} \colon C^{(r)}(k) \to J(k)$ containing $D$ can be identified with
the linear system $|D|$. More precisely, the fibre of the map of functors
$C^{(r)} \to J$ is the functor $\Div_C^D$ of (3.14); therefore the fibre of
$f^{(r)}$ containing $D$ (in the sense of algebraic spaces) is a copy of
projective space of dimension $h^0(D) - 1$. Corollary 3.10 of Chapter I shows
that conversely every copy of projective space in $C^{(r)}$ is contained in
some fibre of $f^{(r)}$. Consequently, the closed points of the Jacobian can
be identified with the set of maximal subvarieties of $C^{(r)}$ isomorphic to
projective space.

Note that for $r > 2g - 2$, $|D|$ has dimension $r - g$, and so
$(df^{(r)})_D$ is surjective, for all $D$. Therefore $f^{(r)}$ is smooth (see
Hartshorne 1977, III 10.4), and the fibres of $f^{(r)}$ are precisely the
copies of $\mathbb{P}^{r-g}$ contained in $C^{(r)}$. This last observation is
the starting point of Chow's construction of the Jacobian Chow 1954.

\section*{5 \quad The canonical maps from the symmetric powers of $C$ to its
Jacobian variety}

Throughout this section $C$ will be a complete nonsingular curve of genus
$g > 0$. Assume there is a $k$-rational point $P$ on $C$, and write $f$ for
the map $f^P$ defined in \S 2.

Let $f^r$ be the map $C^r \to J$ sending $(P_1, \dots, P_r)$ to
$f(P_1) + \dots + f(P_r)$. On points, $f^r$ is the map
$(P_1, \dots, P_r) \mapsto [P_1 + \dots + P_r - rP]$. Clearly it is
symmetric, and so induces a map $f^{(r)} \colon C^{(r)} \to J$. We can regard
$f^{(r)}$ as being the map sending an effective divisor $D$ of degree $r$ on
$C$ to the linear equivalence class of $D - rP$. The fibre of the map
$f^{(r)} \colon C^{(r)}(k) \to J(k)$ containing $D$ can be identified with the
space of effective divisors linearly equivalent to $D$, that is, with the
linear system $|D|$. The image of $C^{(r)}$ in $J$ is a closed subvariety
$W^r$ of $J$, which can also be written $W^r = f(C) + \dots + f(C)$ ($r$
summands).

\paragraph{Theorem 5.1.}
\textit{(a) For all $r \le g$, the morphism $f^{(r)} \colon C^{(r)} \to W^r$
is birational; in particular, $f^{(g)}$ is a birational map from $C^{(g)}$
onto $J$.}

\textit{(b) Let $D$ be an effective divisor of degree $r$ on $C$, and let $F$
be the fibre of $f^{(r)}$ containing $D$. Then no tangent vector to $C^{(r)}$
at $D$ maps to zero under $(df^{(r)})_D$ unless it lies in the direction of
$F$; in other words, the sequence}
\[
  0 \to T_D(F) \to T_D(C^{(r)}) \to T_a(J), \quad a = f^{(r)}(D),
\]
\textit{is exact. In particular,
$(df^{(r)})_D \colon T_D(C^{(r)}) \to T_a(J)$ is injective if $|D|$ has
dimension zero.}

The proof will occupy the rest of this section.

For $D$ a divisor on $C$, we write $h^0(D)$ for the dimension of
\[
  H^0(C, \mathcal{L}(D)) = \{ f \in k(C) \mid (f) + D \ge 0 \}
\]
and $h^1(D)$ for the dimension of $H^1(C, \mathcal{L}(D))$. Recall that
\[
  h^0(D) - h^1(D) = \deg(D) + 1 - g,
\]
and that $H^1(C, \mathcal{L}(D))^{\vee} = H^0(C, \Omega^1(-D))$, which can be
identified with the set of $\omega \in \Omega^1_{k(C)/k}$ whose divisor
$(\omega) \ge D$.

\paragraph{Lemma 5.2.}
\textit{(a) Let $D$ be a divisor on $C$ such that $h^1(D) > 0$; then there is
a nonempty open subset $U$ of $C$ such that $h^1(D + Q) = h^1(D) - 1$ for all
points $Q$ in $U$, and $h^1(D + Q) = h^1(D)$ for $Q \notin U$.}

\textit{(b) For any $r \le g$, there is an open subset $U$ of $C^r$ such that
$h^0(\sum P_i) = 1$ for all $(P_1, \dots, P_r)$ in $U$.}

\section*{6 \quad The Jacobian variety as Albanese variety; autoduality}

Throughout this section $C$ will be a complete nonsingular curve of genus
$g > 0$ over a field $k$, and $J$ will be its Jacobian variety.

\paragraph{Proposition 6.1.}
\textit{Let $P$ be a $k$-rational point on $C$. The map
$f^P \colon C \to J$ has the following universal property: for any map
$\varphi \colon C \to A$ from $C$ into an abelian variety sending $P$ to $0$,
there is a unique homomorphism $\psi \colon J \to A$ such that
$\varphi = \psi \circ f^P$.}

\paragraph{Proof.}
Consider the map
\[
  (P_1, \dots, P_g) \mapsto \sum_i \psi(P_i) \colon C^g \to A.
  % [sic: printed "\psi(P_i)"; presumably "\varphi(P_i)" is intended, since \psi is being constructed]
\]
Clearly this is symmetric, and so it factors through $C^{(g)}$. It therefore
defines a rational map $\psi \colon J \to A$, which (I 3.2) shows to be a
regular map. It is clear from the construction that $\psi \circ f^P = \varphi$
(note that $f^P$ is the composite of
$Q \mapsto Q + (g-1)P \colon C \to C^{(g)}$ with
$f^{(g)} \colon C^{(g)} \to J$). In particular, $\psi$ maps $0$ to $0$, and
(I 1.2) shows that it is therefore a homomorphism. If $\psi'$ is a second
homomorphism such that $\psi' \circ f^P = \varphi$, then $\psi$ and $\psi'$
agree on $f^P(C) + \dots + f^P(C)$ ($g$ copies), which is the whole of $J$.
\hfill $\square$

\paragraph{Corollary 6.2.}
\textit{Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a divisorial correspondence between $(C, P)$ and
$J$ such that $(1 \times f^P)^* \mathcal{N} \approx \mathcal{L}^P$; then
$\mathcal{N} \approx \mathcal{M}^P$ (notations as in \S 2 and (1.7)).}

\paragraph{Proof.}
Because of (I 5.13), we can assume $k$ to be algebraically closed. According
to (1.7) there is a unique map $\varphi \colon J \to J$ such that
$\mathcal{N} \approx (1 \times \varphi)^* \mathcal{M}^P$. On points $\varphi$
is the map sending $a \in J(k)$ to the unique $b$ such that
$\mathcal{M}^P | C \times \{b\} \approx \mathcal{N} | C \times \{a\}$. By
assumption,
\[
  \mathcal{N} | C \times \{f^P Q\}
  \approx \mathcal{L}^P | C \times \{Q\}
  \approx \mathcal{M}^P | C \times \{f^P Q\},
\]
and so $(\varphi \circ f^P)(Q) = f^P(Q)$ for all $Q$. Now (6.1) shows that
$f$ is the identity map. % [sic: printed "$f$"; presumably "\varphi" is intended]
\hfill $\square$

\paragraph{Corollary 6.3.}
\textit{Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ be curves over $k$ with $k$-rational points $P_1$
and $P_2$, and let $J_1$ and $J_2$ be their Jacobians. There is a one-to-one
correspondence between $\Hom_k(J_1, J_2)$ and the set of isomorphism classes
of divisorial correspondences between $(C_1, P_1)$ and $(C_2, P_2)$.}

\paragraph{Proof.}
A divisorial correspondence between $(C_2, P_2)$ and $(C_1, P_1)$ gives rise
to a morphism $(C_1, P_1) \to J_2$ (by 1.7), and this morphism gives rise to
homomorphism $J_1 \to J_2$ (by 6.1). % [sic: printed "gives rise to homomorphism", missing "a"]
Conversely, a homomorphism $\psi \colon J_1 \to J_2$ defines a divisorial
correspondence $(1 \times (f^{P_1} \circ \psi))^* \mathcal{M}^{P_2}$ between
$(C_2, P_2)$ and $(C_1, P_1)$.
\hfill $\square$

In the case that $C$ has a point $P$ rational over $k$, define
$F \colon C \times C \to J$ to be the map
$(P_1, P_2) \mapsto f^P(P_1) - f^P(P_2)$. One checks immediately that this is
independent of the choice of $P$. Thus, if $P \in C(k')$ for some Galois
extension $k'$ of $k$, and $F \colon C_{k'} \times C_{k'} \to J_{k'}$ is the
corresponding map, then $\sigma F = F$ for all
$\sigma \in \Gal(k'/k)$; therefore $F$ is defined over $k$ whether or not $C$
has a $k$-rational point. Note that it is zero on the diagonal $\Delta$ of
$C \times C$.
